Welcome, Congressman.

turn_text: George McGovern got interested in this issue after watching a documentary on CBS back in the late 1960s called Hunger in America. And he was watching with his family and there was a scene of a young kid in school who didn't have anything to eat and the reporter asked the young boy, what's wrong? He says, I don't have any to eat and I'm ashamed. And George McGovern said, well, it's me, a United States senator, we should be ashamed that we would tolerate a system that would allow a little boy to be hungry in school. And so he helped form a special select committee on nutrition and human needs that he and other senators like Bob Dole, Republican, they did hearings all around the country exposing the problem of hunger. And then that led to a White House conference on food and nutrition that paved the way to expand the the Food Stamp Program, now known as SNAP, establishing the WIC Program, Women's Infants and Children Program, expanding school nutrition programs. And we made progress in the 1970s trying to eradicate hunger. And then in the 1980s, we began to backslide. In the 1990s, we did. And then here we are today with 40 million people who don't know where the next meal is going to come from. This really is about political will and about making this a priority issue. And so George McGovern, I sat through a lot of those hearings in his special select committee, and I felt his passion that we ought to end it. If you ever seen a hungry child that breaks your heart.

turn_text: There are a lot of things. One is obviously, you know, lack of adequate income. And one of the stereotypes out there is that people who are hungry are people who somehow don't have a job. Well, a majority of people who are right now on SNAP. who are able to work actually do work, but they get paid so little they still qualify for the benefit. So just having a job in and of itself doesn't necessarily protect you from hunger. We have a lot of companies that pay really lousy wages, and we need to do something about that. Sometimes people are hungry because they, you know, fall on hard times, medical emergencies, and they don't have the money to be able to you know, pay for food. Sometimes people are hungry because they live in places like food deserts. They don't have access to good nutritious food. I mean, there's a whole bunch of reasons why, but not withstanding that. of the reasons why people are hungry can't be fixed, can't be solved. And, you know, some people will criticize me and say, well, you know, you just want to throw more money at the problem. Yeah, I do want to invest more money to make sure that everybody has access to good, nutritious food. But to do nothing, to maintain the status quo is terribly costly. The costs are astronomical in terms of avoidable health care issues that spring up because of food insecurity and hunger. Senior citizens show up in emergency rooms because they're supposed to take their medicine with a meal, but they can't afford both. So they take their medicine on every stomach. You're not a productive worker in the workplace if you're hungry. Kids who go to school who are hungry can't learn. That meal is everybody's important to that child's ability to learn as a textbook or a laptop. There's cost to all of this and not having access to good nutrition. Again, they develop chronic diseases that are with you for your life. So all of the challenges around hunger can be solved. The question is whether we're gonna have the political will to solve it.
